name: Modern B2B SaaS
tagline: Multi-tenant subscription software with real customers and real audits
summary: A stack for software sold to companies: tenant isolation, role-based access, audit trails, background work and enough observability to answer "what happened to this customer at 14:07?". It grows from the MVP stack by adding a cache, a broker and infrastructure automation.
basis: TechFlow archetype, not a specific company's stack. It reflects the components most B2B products converge on once they have paying tenants and compliance questions.

items.note: Component model plus server rendering for the marketing and app surfaces.
Static assets, TLS termination and bot filtering at the edge.
One entry point for auth, quotas and routing.
Per-tenant limits so one customer's batch job cannot starve the rest.
Modules per domain; extract a service only when a team or scaling need demands it.
Shapes data for the web app without leaking internal models.
Public API surface customers integrate against.
Customers upgrade on their schedule, not yours.
Tenant-scoped rows with row-level security or a schema per tenant.
Sessions, permission lookups and hot reads via Cache Aside.
Customer files and exports; never on the application disk.
Emails, exports, webhooks and imports off the request path.
Events published only when the database transaction commits.
Signed, retried callbacks so customers can react to changes.
SSO is a procurement requirement, not a nice-to-have.
Roles per tenant; permissions checked server-side on every call.
Short-lived access tokens for service-to-service and API clients.
Tests, migrations and deploys on every merge.
Environments are reviewable code, not console clicks.
Release without a maintenance window; roll back by switching traffic.
One trace per request across app, cache and broker.
Availability targets you can hold yourself to in a contract.

whenToUse: You sell to companies and must isolate tenants from each other
Customers ask about SSO, audit logs, uptime and data residency
Background work (exports, imports, webhooks) has become significant
The team is large enough to own deployment and monitoring
tradeoffs: Every added component is another thing to patch, monitor and pay for
Per-tenant isolation complicates migrations, backups and noisy-neighbour handling
A broker plus a cache means eventual consistency shows up in the product
Infrastructure automation is a real investment before it saves time
